title: Who is using claude opus with unreal blueprint? Is it pointless? I'm enjoying it.
author: Afraid-Fly-7030
selftext:
I've always dabbled a bit in unreal over the years but never made much headway. I work in vfx so the workflows are not completely alien to me but as a software it's quite confusing how stuff is put together as I dig into it.

Recently I've been using Claude to help put together logic and systems with blueprints and then giving me a step by step walkthrough to learn from. I find it really enjoyable and love the ability to get it to create settings so I can dial in very specific details. (As a test project what I'm making could be considered souls-like combat - lock on, attack, dodge.)

But I'm seeing a lot games here that look very advanced and I wonder if it's the wrong approach.

I really want to be able to dial in tiny details, like animation cancel windows, retiming animations at certain points to enhance impact, scaling/adjusting hitboxes, adjusting the anim so the hand fits perfectly on the weapon. In these 'one shot' or multiple prompt games do the developers control the minute details of things happening to dial in the game feel or are they essentially a black box that they rely on prompts to get it feeling right.

I'm enjoying my current workflow to learn but also realise Unreal are planning on phasing out blueprints entirely at some point and maybe it's a waste learning this way. 

To have granular control in an AI-developed game would it be best to rely on C++/code for each system and instead have it create gui's/settings for each system? What I like about blueprints is the visual nature of it and being able to clearly read what's happening (although I find it a bit annoying sometimes jumping between different blueprints constantly.)

comments.author: GaussRausch
comments.body:
I’m working on Elysium, reconstructing Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines in Unreal. All the code is written by AI agents. My role is direction, architecture, deciding what correct behaviour means, and reviewing/testing the results.

I mainly use C++ for gameplay systems and Python for the asset pipeline. C++ is convenient for agents because they can read the implementation, review diffs, make changes and run tests. I also use Animation Blueprints with custom C++ nodes.

You can have AI author Blueprints directly, too. There are a few routes:

\- \*\*MCP:\*\* Connect your agent to an Unreal MCP integration that exposes Blueprint graph tools. It can create Blueprints, add nodes and variables, and connect pins, leaving you with a visual graph to inspect and edit. Available operations depend on the integration; \[this Unreal MCP project\](https://github.com/voodoofox/unreal-mcp/blob/main/Docs/Tools/README.md) documents those tools.  
\- \*\*Unreal’s Python integration:\*\* Have the agent write scripts that run inside the editor to automate asset creation and configuration. I use this extensively. Some graph operations need a C++ helper exposed to Python, which I had the agents build for my Animation Blueprint importer. \[Epic documents the editor Python workflow here.\](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/scripting-the-unreal-editor-using-python)  
\- \*\*Plain-text graph files:\*\* Unreal’s Blueprint copy/paste format is text. In Elysium, I store my animation graph in a \`.t3d\` file, then use Python and a C++ helper to import it, compile the Blueprint and save the asset. I can also edit the graph visually, copy its nodes and save that text back into the repository. That gives the agent reviewable text while preserving the visual authoring workflow.

Your idea of having AI build systems with exposed controls is very close to what I do. I have Unreal settings pages and a dedicated “Green Room” where I can scrub animations, change playback speed and adjust layer weights. I’ve also had the agents build checks that measure whether the rendered weapon follows the character’s hand correctly.

For your combat prototype, I’d ask it to implement explicit controls for cancel windows, hitbox dimensions and playback timing, plus debug views so you can see what’s happening. Those details still need deliberate testing and tuning, even when AI writes the implementation.

And I wouldn’t abandon Blueprints over the phasing-out claim. \[Epic’s current documentation\](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/coding-in-unreal-engine-blueprint-vs-cplusplus) recommends combining C++ and Blueprints. You can keep the visual workflow you enjoy and move particular systems into C++ as needed.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: Unreal is removing Blueprints in next version (6) and committing to a more AI focused workflow with Verse. I wouldn't go diving into learning Blueprint unless you plan on sticking with old versions of the engine going forward. Seems like a waste of your time and energy and will largely fall to the wayside as AI becomes even more of a focus for implementation.
